newsitem.title: UK: World LPG trade muted by US slump, high Saudi price.
newsitem.headline: World LPG trade muted by US slump, high Saudi price.

text.p: A dramatic slump in the U.S. Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) market triggered a gentle softening of European prices this week, but traders said that tight fundamentals and strong prices in the Middle East are expected to limit the downside.
The recent collapse in U.S. prices from six year highs brought about a nervousness in the European market and stifled trade, dealers said.
While prices were off their highs of the previous week, which saw a propane large ship trade as high as $367 cif NWE, traders said that prices had notionally stabilised in the $350s.
"Not many deals were done, but the market seems to have settled and should be able to sustain these levels for the time-being," said one Scandinavian large ships trader.
A propane cargo traded on Thursday at $355 a tonne cif France while coasters were assessed in the low $340s fob U.K.
Butane coasters were assessed steady at $270/$275 a tonne.
Despite historically low stock levels, U.S. prices slumped as a combination of mild weather and year-end profit-taking triggered a big sell-off.
Prices at the Gulf Coast trading hub of Mont Belvieu shed 15 cents a gallon, or $75/$80 a tonne over the last 10 days.
"The U.S. market has been on the rise for months...A lot of people were sitting on huge profits which they wanted to get hold of before the end of the year," said one trader.
In the Middle East, traders said that Saudi Aramco's first January tender, the T1 tender, was awarded at a bullish $345/$348 a tonne for propane and $350 for butane.

The tender award indicates that the January Saudi CP -- the benchmark for most Asian LPG trades --- was likely to climb further than the record highs of $310 for propane and butane posted for December.
The world's largest LPG supplier Saudi Aramco sets its LPG contract prices based on the company's own assessments of spot market trends as well as the results of the three monthly tenders.
"The high CP is really frightening off buyers," said a trader for an international major.
Japanese prices were pegged at a softer premium of $45/$50 a tonne to the CP, but traders said buyers were still reluctant to lift at current levels.
Japan's Agency of Natural Resources and Energy said on Friday that it has relaxed the requirements on mandatory LPG stockpiles.

Importers have been calling for a relaxation of the law -- which requires them to maintain stockpiles equivalent to 50 days of imports -- in order to avoid setting a bullish tone in the market by buying spot cargoes at current high prices.
The government will now allow importers to borrow cargoes from other buyers to meet the required volumes, an agency spokesman said.
"This gives the market some weak mood," said one trader.
In the Middle East itself, fob premiums were talked steady to slightly firmer at CP +$30/$35 a tonne, fob Gulf.
--Rosalind Russell, London Newsroom +44 171 542 5387 (c) Reuters Limited 1996
